metadata.title: The development of ICT skills in adolescence at the intersection of gender and family background

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Grade 9 and higher) two-wave longitudinal data for Germany, with ICT skills measured in grade 9 (wave 1) and grade 12 (wave 7). The analytic sample is restricted to students in regular secondary schools (excluding special needs schools and cases with missing grade-9 ICT skills; and excluding non-academic-track students from grade-12 growth analyses due to high missingness). The manuscript does not report applying NEPS complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight scheme; instead, it uses cluster-robust (Huber-White sandwich) standard errors at the school level. Because the analysis is regression-based (not ML) and the paper does not specify weight variables, weighting strategy details are not available from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used NEPS Starting Cohort 4 two-wave data on ICT skills for Germany. Included ninth-grade secondary school students in 648 schools; excluded 1532 students attending special needs schools or with unknown school type (needed to separate academic vs non-academic tracks). Excluded 737 students lacking grade-9 ICT skills (critical predictor for grade-12 change in the imputation model). Removed 19 students with missing migration background. For ICT skill growth analyses, restricted grade-12 change to the academic track only because of very high missing ICT skill information at the second measurement point for non-academic-track students; ICT skills at grade 12 were imputed only for academic-track students.

main_findings.dataset_used: NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) Grade 9 ICT skills (wave 1, 2010/11)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression coefficients with cluster-robust SEs; standardized continuous variables. Key reported effects: Female vs male B = −0.05* (non-academic) and −0.11*** (academic). Language use (mostly German reference) B = −0.29*** (non-academic) and −0.33*** (academic). Books at home B = 0.20*** (non-academic) and 0.18*** (academic). Income (ln) B = 0.11*** (non-academic) and 0.02 (academic).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) Grade 9 ICT skills the study leveraged Gender, Language use at home, Highest parental education, Number of books at home, and Household equivalence income to predict ICT skills in grade 9 (WLE), finding that ICT skills are lower for females and for students who do not predominantly speak German at home, while more books at home are associated with higher ICT skills. This indicates that early ICT-skill inequalities by gender and family resources are already present in grade 9 and should be addressed through targeted support for girls and students from linguistically and socioeconomically disadvantaged homes.

main_findings.dataset_used: NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) ICT skills growth Grade 9 to Grade 12 (wave 1 to wave 7, academic track only)
main_findings.target_variable: ICT skills change from grade 9 to grade 12 (WLE)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression coefficients with cluster-robust SEs; 60 imputations; standardized continuous variables. Key reported effects: Male vs female growth B = −0.28*** (academic; female reference in tables). Grade 9 ICT skills predicting change B = 0.54***. Interaction patterns: gender gap in growth decreases with income and disappears for incomes > +2 SD (interaction not statistically significant at mean levels); no significant interactions for parental education, books, or family language on growth (Table A2–A4).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) Grade 9 to Grade 12 ICT skills growth data (restricted to the academic track), the study leveraged Gender, Grade 9 ICT skills, and family background indicators to predict ICT skills change, finding that the gender gap in favor of males increases over time but is smaller for higher-income students and shows no statistically significant moderation by parental education, books at home, or family language. This indicates that interventions should prioritize sustaining ICT-skill development for girls in academic-track schooling, while also considering that economic resources may buffer gender gaps in ICT growth.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) longitudinal ICT skills measured in paper-pencil multiple-choice tests in grade 9 (wave 1, 2010/11) and grade 12 (wave 7, 2013/14). The analytic sample includes 14,137 ninth-graders in Germany across 523 schools, with grade-12 growth restricted to the academic track due to high missingness in the non-academic track; missing ICT data were handled via two-level multiple imputation (60 imputations) using Blimp 3.1 with random intercepts. ICT skills are scaled using Warm’s mean-weighted likelihood estimator (WLE) from an IRT model (WLE reliability: 0.81 in grade 9; 0.73 in grade 12). Results show small but consistent male advantages in grade-9 ICT skills (e.g., female vs male B = −0.05* non-academic; −0.11*** academic) and a larger male advantage in growth (female vs male B = −0.28*** in academic track), with the gender gap in growth decreasing as income increases. Limitations include the absence of ML modeling/metrics (the paper uses regression with interactions) and no explicit reporting of survey-weight application in the provided text.
